question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
answer:
You control exactly one of your opponent's turns, you do get a second Emrakul, the Promised End (as a token), but that second Emrakul does NOT generate another "gain control" trigger — however, the opponent still ends up taking two extra turns.

Here's the breakdown:

1) The trigger copy. When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, its "When you cast this spell, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn" ability goes on the stack. Lithoform Engine's first ability copies that triggered ability (707.10), putting a second copy of it on the stack above the original. You now have two separate instances of that ability, both targeting the same opponent (since you didn't indicate choosing a new target, and in a two-player game there's only one legal target anyway).

2) Resolution order and the control effect. The copy (created more recently) sits on top of the stack and resolves first; the original trigger resolves after it. Each resolution creates its own "gain control ... during that player's next turn" effect and schedules its own "after that turn, extra turn" effect. Per Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14, when multiple player-controlling effects target the same player for the same turn, they overwrite each other and only the last-created one actually works — but each triggered ability's resolution still independently creates its own extra-turn effect. So: you end up controlling the opponent's next turn only once (the effect from whichever trigger resolved last, here the original cast trigger, is the one that actually takes hold), but the opponent gets two extra turns afterward (rule 500.7 — extra turns are added one at a time, with the most recently created one taken first, so the two extra turns stack up back-to-back after the turn you controlled).

3) The permanent-spell copy. Lithoform Engine's third-mode ability targets Emrakul, the Promised End itself (still on the stack as a spell) and creates a copy of it. Per rule 111.13, a copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves, with the copied object's characteristics — so you get a second 13/13 flying, trample, protection-from-instants Emrakul, the Promised End as a token, in addition to the real Emrakul that resolves normally afterward (since that copy is on top of the stack, it resolves before the original spell does). You end up with two Emrakuls on the battlefield: one real, one a token copy.

4) No extra "gain control" trigger from the spell copy. Emrakul, the Promised End's control-changing ability triggers "when you cast this spell." Copying a spell is explicitly not casting it (rule 707.10: "a copy of a spell isn't cast"; see also Lithoform Engine ruling #6, which states directly that creating a copy this way won't cause abilities that trigger on casting a spell or activating an ability to trigger). So the copied Emrakul resolving into a token does not add a third "gain control" trigger — you only ever had the two triggers from step 1 (the original cast trigger and Lithoform Engine's copy of it).

Net result: 2 Emrakuls on the battlefield (one real, one token), you control 1 of your opponent's turns, and your opponent takes 2 extra turns afterward. I'm assuming a two-player game (single defending player) and that no new target was chosen for the copied trigger; in a multiplayer game the outcome is the same as long as both trigger instances target the same single opponent, since the overwrite/extra-turn mechanics in rule 500.7 and Emrakul ruling #14 don't depend on total player count.

cited_text.707.10: To copy a spell, activated ability, or triggered ability means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated. A copy of a spell or ability copies both the characteristics of the spell or ability and all decisions made for it, including modes, targets, the value of X, and additional or alternative costs. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) Choices that are normally made on resolution are not copied. If an effect of the copy refers to objects used to pay its costs, it uses the objects used to pay the costs of the original spell or ability. A copy of a spell is owned by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell or ability is controlled by the player under whose control it was put on the stack. A copy of a spell is itself a spell, even though it has no spell card associated with it. A copy of an ability is itself an ability. A player casts Fork, targeting an Emerald Charm. Fork reads, “Copy target instant or sorcery spell, except that the copy is red. You may choose new targets for the copy.” Emerald Charm is a modal green instant. When the Fork resolves, it puts a copy of the Emerald Charm on the stack except the copy is red, not green. The copy has the same mode that was chosen for the original Emerald Charm. It does not necessarily have the same target, but only because Fork allows choosing of new targets. Fling is an instant that reads, “As an additional cost to cast this spell, sacrifice a creature” and “Fling deals damage equal to the sacrificed creature’s power to any target.” When determining how much damage a copy of Fling deals, it checks the power of the creature sacrificed to pay for the original Fling. Dawnglow Infusion is a sorcery that reads, “You gain X life if {G} was spent to cast this spell and X life if {W} was spent to cast it.” Because mana isn’t an object, a copy of Dawnglow Infusion won’t cause you to gain any life, no matter what mana was spent to cast the original spell.
cited_text.111.13: A copy of a permanent spell becomes a token as it resolves. The token has the characteristics of the spell that became that token. The token is not “created” for the purposes of any replacement effects or triggered abilities that refer to creating a token.
cited_text.500.7: Some effects can give a player extra turns. They do this by adding the turns directly after the specified turn. If a player is given multiple extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time. If multiple players are given extra turns, the extra turns are added one at a time, in APNAP order (see rule 101.4). The most recently created turn will be taken first.
cited_text.601.1: Previously, the action of casting a spell, or casting a card as a spell, was referred to on cards as “playing” that spell or that card. Cards that were printed with that text have received errata in the Oracle card reference so they now refer to “casting” that spell or that card.

question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
answer:
With X=0, Awaken the Woods costs a total of {1}{G}{G} (3 mana: 2 green plus 1 generic payable in any color) and creates 0 Forest Dryad tokens — you'd be paying full Trinisphere price for nothing. You should instead choose X=2: that also costs a total of {1}{G}{G} (3 mana) but nets you 2 Forest Dryad land creature tokens, since Trinisphere's price floor is being paid either way.

Here's the math. Awaken the Woods' mana cost is {X}{G}{G} (rule 107.3a: since Awaken the Woods' text doesn't define X, you as its controller choose and announce X as part of casting it, per 601.2b). With X=0, the mana cost as announced is {0}{G}{G} — effectively {G}{G}, 2 mana total, 0 of it generic.

Per 601.2f, you build the total cost by starting from the mana/alternative cost, applying cost increases and additional costs, then applying cost reductions (which can't take the generic portion below {0}), and finally applying any remaining cost-changing effects like Trinisphere's, then locking the total in. Your "green spells cost {1} less" reduction only touches the generic portion of the cost. At X=0 there is no generic mana to reduce (it's already {0}), so the reduction does nothing — you're still looking at {G}{G} (2 mana total) after reductions.

Then Trinisphere applies: "each spell that would cost less than three mana to cast costs three mana to cast" (Trinisphere's card text overrides the normal cost math where relevant). Trinisphere's own ruling confirms the order: lock in mana/alternative cost, apply increases/reductions, then apply Trinisphere's floor if the mana component is still under three mana [Trinisphere ruling #0]. Since {G}{G} is only 2 mana, Trinisphere bumps the total to 3 mana, with the extra 1 mana payable in any color. Final total cost at X=0: {1}{G}{G} (2 green + 1 generic of any color) for 0 tokens. That's rule 601.2f for the reduction floor and Trinisphere's own text/ruling for the floor-to-three effect.

Now compare X=2: the mana cost is {2}{G}{G} (4 mana: 2 generic + 2 green). Your reduction removes {1} generic mana (per 601.2f, reductions apply to the generic portion), giving {1}{G}{G} (3 mana). Since 3 mana is not less than three mana, Trinisphere's floor doesn't add anything further [Trinisphere ruling #0]. Final total cost: {1}{G}{G} (3 mana total, same as the X=0 case), and since X=2 was the announced/locked-in value for the spell on the stack (107.3a, 107.3c), you create 2 Forest Dryad tokens.

So X=0 and X=1 both waste mana against Trinisphere's floor (paying 3 mana for 0 or 1 tokens), while X=2 is the breakeven point where you get the most value for that same floor price — 2 tokens for 3 mana. Beyond X=2, the reduction is already fully used up, so each additional point of X simply adds 1 mana to the total for 1 more token (e.g., X=3 costs {2}{G}{G} = 4 mana for 3 tokens), a normal 1-for-1 rate. Given that, X=2 is the minimum sensible choice to avoid wasting mana; going higher is fine if you have the mana to spare, but there's no more hidden "free" value beyond that point.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).

cited_text.601.2f: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). The player determines the total cost of the spell. Usually this is just the mana cost. Some spells have additional or alternative costs. Some effects may increase or reduce the cost to pay, or may provide other alternative costs. Costs may include paying mana, tapping permanents, sacrificing permanents, discarding cards, and so on. The total cost is the mana cost or alternative cost (as determined in rule 601.2b), plus all additional costs and cost increases, and minus all cost reductions. If multiple cost reductions apply, the player may apply them in any order. If the mana component of the total cost is reduced to nothing by cost reduction effects, it is considered to be {0}. It can’t be reduced to less than {0}. Once the total cost is determined, any effects that directly affect the total cost are applied. Then the resulting total cost becomes “locked in.” If effects would change the total cost after this time, they have no effect.
cited_text.601.2b: To cast a spell is to take it from where it is (usually the hand), put it on the stack, and pay its costs, so that it will eventually resolve and have its effect. Casting a spell includes proposal of the spell (rules 601.2a–d) and determination and payment of costs (rules 601.2f–h). To cast a spell, a player follows the steps listed below, in order. A player must be legally allowed to cast the spell to begin this process (see rule 601.3). If a player is unable to comply with the requirements of a step listed below while performing that step, the casting of the spell is illegal; the game returns to the moment before the casting of that spell was proposed (see rule 733, “Handling Illegal Actions”). If the spell is modal, the player announces the mode choice (see rule 700.2). If the player wishes to splice any cards onto the spell (see rule 702.47), they reveal those cards in their hand. If the spell has alternative or additional costs that will be paid as it’s being cast such as buyback or kicker costs (see rules 118.8 and 118.9), the player announces their intentions to pay any or all of those costs (see rule 601.2f). A player can’t apply two alternative methods of casting or two alternative costs to a single spell. If the spell has a variable cost that will be paid as it’s being cast (such as an {X} in its mana cost; see rule 107.3), the player announces the value of that variable. If the value of that variable is defined in the text of the spell by a choice that player would make later in the announcement or resolution of the spell, that player makes that choice at this time instead of that later time. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes hybrid mana symbols, the player announces the nonhybrid equivalent cost they intend to pay. If a cost that will be paid as the spell is being cast includes Phyrexian mana symbols, the player announces whether they intend to pay 2 life or a corresponding colored mana cost for each of those symbols. Previously made choices (such as choosing to cast a spell with flashback from a graveyard or choosing to cast a creature with morph face down) may restrict the player’s options when making these choices.
cited_text.107.3a: Many objects use the letter X as a placeholder for a number that needs to be determined. Some objects have abilities that define the value of X; the rest let their controller choose the value of X. If a spell or activated ability has a mana cost, alternative cost, additional cost, and/or activation cost with an {X}, [-X], or X in it, and the value of X isn’t defined by the text of that spell or ability, the controller of that spell or ability chooses and announces the value of X as part of casting the spell or activating the ability. (See rule 601, “Casting Spells.”) While a spell is on the stack, any X in its mana cost or in any alternative cost or additional cost it has equals the announced value. While an activated ability is on the stack, any X in its activation cost equals the announced value.
cited_text.107.3c: Many objects use the letter X as a placeholder for a number that needs to be determined. Some objects have abilities that define the value of X; the rest let their controller choose the value of X. If a spell or activated ability has an {X}, [-X], or X in its cost and/or its text, and the value of X is defined by the text of that spell or ability, then that’s the value of X while that spell or ability is on the stack. The controller of that spell or ability doesn’t get to choose the value. Note that the value of X may change while that spell or ability is on the stack.

question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
answer:
Yes, you can target Grist, the Hunger Tide with Animate Dead while Grist, the Hunger Tide is in your graveyard, but the result is that Grist, the Hunger Tide ends up back in your graveyard almost immediately, sacrificed rather than kept.

Here's why: Animate Dead's enchant restriction is "enchant creature card in a graveyard." Per Grist, the Hunger Tide's own printed text, "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types," and Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1 confirms that anywhere but the battlefield it is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect. So while it's in the graveyard, Grist, the Hunger Tide is a valid creature card for Animate Dead to enchant, and you can cast Animate Dead targeting it.

When Animate Dead resolves, its triggered ability fires: "Return enchanted creature card to the battlefield under your control and attach this Aura to it." Grist, the Hunger Tide comes back under your control and Animate Dead attaches to it (Animate Dead ruling #1). But the instant Grist, the Hunger Tide is on the battlefield, its own text means it is *no longer* a creature — it's just a planeswalker. That means Animate Dead is now attached to a permanent it can't legally enchant (Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature anymore).

This is exactly the situation described in Animate Dead ruling #4: if the returned card can't legally be enchanted by Animate Dead (there, protection from black is the example; here, the object simply isn't a creature), Animate Dead is put into your graveyard as a state-based action. That triggers Animate Dead's delayed ability, "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it." When that delayed trigger resolves, since Grist, the Hunger Tide is still on the battlefield (now as a planeswalker), you must sacrifice it.

Net effect: Grist, the Hunger Tide briefly enters the battlefield under your control (getting a moment where you could theoretically respond to the delayed sacrifice trigger, e.g. activate a loyalty ability if you have priority before the trigger resolves), but it will then be sacrificed and go back to your graveyard as a state-based action forces Animate Dead off and its leaves-the-battlefield trigger forces the sacrifice. Card text (Grist, the Hunger Tide's creature-while-not-on-battlefield clause, and Animate Dead's own enchant/attach/leaves-battlefield text) overrides the general assumption that a returned creature stays a creature, which is why this interaction plays out differently than animating an ordinary creature card.

Assumption: this analysis assumes no other effects (like something granting Grist, the Hunger Tide creature type while on the battlefield) are in play; if such an effect existed, Animate Dead could remain legally attached.
